Squid proxy initiating outbound FTP control-channel (TCP/21) to external host (Squidbleed precondition) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the exploitation precondition for Squidbleed (CVE-2026-47729): a Squid proxy coaxed by a trusted client into opening an FTP control connection to an attacker-controlled server on port 21. Surfaces Squid-process-initiated TCP/21 egress to public IPs, the only network shape the over-read exploit can use. Rationale: Anchored on the article's hard precondition — Squid reaching an attacker FTP server on TCP/21 (default-on per Calif/THN). The squid-process + port-21 + public-IP triad is the only network shape the over-read can ride; verified against Calif's disclosure and Horizon3.ai write-up. Datadog left empty: Linux netconn for a daemon isn't cleanly carried by the standard linux.auditd/syslog sources. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/squidbleed-cve-2026-47729 • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-47729/ • https://securityonline.info/squidbleed-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1071.002 T1212
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FTP mirror/package downloads proxied through Squid (ftp.debian.org, archive.ubuntu.com)
  • CI/build agents pulling artifacts from public FTP repos via the corporate proxy
  • Network monitoring or uptime probes hitting external FTP servers
  • A legacy line-of-business app still transferring files over FTP through the proxy
  • Vendor data feeds delivered over anonymous FTP
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has_any ("ftp.debian.org","ftp.gnu.org","archive.ubuntu.com","ftp.freebsd.org")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal client whose request drove the FTP fetch (proxy access log SourceIP/user) and reputation-check the external FTP destination — newly-registered/unattributed IP on port 21 is the red flag. 2) Contain: if the destination is unknown/hostile, block egress TCP/21 from the proxy at the firewall and set Squid `acl` to deny ftp:// (or `ftp_passive`/protocol disable) immediately. 3) Hunt: pull all ftp:// requests from that client over 24h (see harvesting UC), check for repeated listing fetches to the same host, and rotate any session tokens/credentials for users who transited the proxy during the window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "squid"
| where RemotePort == 21
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 21
| where isnotempty(DestinationIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
// SourceIP here is the Squid proxy host reaching out to an external FTP server
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count() by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct, ProcessName
| order by ConnCount desc

High-volume ftp:// listing requests through Squid proxy to single host (Squidbleed memory harvest) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the active-exploitation pattern of Squidbleed: a single trusted client looping many ftp:// requests at one attacker FTP server to over-read and exfiltrate successive 4KB heap buffers containing other users' cleartext HTTP requests, Authorization headers and session tokens. Thresholds on ftp:// request volume to <=2 destinations per 10-minute window. Rationale: Targets the exploit's mechanic that the article makes explicit: each malformed FTP listing leaks only the tail of one reused buffer, so the attacker must loop requests at their own FTP host to harvest meaningful memory. Volume of ftp:// to a single destination (Dests<=2) separates the harvest loop from normal one-off FTP browsing. Defender/Falcon empty: Squid application access logs aren't shipped to MDE or FDR — this lives in proxy log telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/squidbleed-cve-2026-47729 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/29-year-old-squid-proxy-bug-squidbleed.html
ATT&CKT1212 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately browsing/recursing a public FTP directory tree (many listing requests)
  • Automated FTP mirroring or a crawler operating behind the proxy
  • Monitoring tooling polling an FTP server's listing on a tight interval
  • Backup or sync jobs that enumerate an FTP target repeatedly
  • Software repo sync (e.g. rsync-over-FTP fallback) through the proxy
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in ("svc-ftpsync","svc-mirror") and Dests <= 2
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP/user is a single client hammering one external FTP host with listing requests; sample the returned filenames in proxy logs for non-printable/garbage bytes (the over-read returns memory, not real filenames). 2) Contain: block the client's proxy access and deny ftp:// at Squid; null-route the destination FTP IP. 3) Hunt: treat all HTTP (cleartext) and TLS-terminated sessions through that proxy in the window as potentially exposed — rotate session tokens/cookies and credentials for affected users, and grep proxy logs for the same destination from other clients.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL startswith "ftp://"
| summarize FtpReqs=count(), Dests=dcount(DestinationHostName), SampleUrls=make_set(RequestURL, 20) by SourceIP, SourceUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FtpReqs > 20 and Dests <= 2   // 20 ftp listing fetches in 10m to <=2 hosts = over-read harvest loop, not normal FTP browsing
| order by FtpReqs desc
source:linux.syslog squid "ftp://"

| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.dest) as dest_count values(Web.url) as urls from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="ftp://*" by Web.src Web.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 20 AND dest_count <= 2 | sort - count
Squid hosts exposed to Squidbleed (CVE-2026-47729) with FTP attack surface AIExploitation High
Posture hunt surfacing Squid installations flagged vulnerable to CVE-2026-47729 so FTP can be disabled or the FtpGateway.cc backport verified. The article stresses the version number is unreliable (Debian ships 5.7; fix landed in 7.x), so this is a starting inventory for verification, not a closed verdict. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-47729) confirmed across Calif, Horizon3.ai and securityonline. Kept as hunting because the article explicitly warns version strings mislead (distro backports), so output is a verification work-queue: pair with the FTP-egress UC to prioritise Squid hosts that actually allow ftp://. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-47729/ • https://blog.calif.io/p/squidbleed-cve-2026-47729
ATT&CKT1212
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Debian/distro builds whose version string looks vulnerable (Squid 5.7) but carry the backported guard
  • Decommissioned or honeypot Squid instances still inventoried
  • Single-tenant Squid with no other trusted clients (real risk far lower)
  • Squid builds with FTP already disabled in squid.conf (surface removed)
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm FTP is actually reachable (squid.conf allows ftp:// and egress TCP/21) — if FTP is off, risk is already removed. 2) Contain: disable FTP in Squid (remove ftp:// from allowed protocols / block port 21) as the article's recommended free mitigation, then schedule the patch. 3) Hunt: verify the fix at source — confirm the null-terminator guard before strchr in FtpGateway.cc or the distro backport, not the version number; cross-check flagged hosts against the FTP-egress and ftp:// harvest UCs for any in-progress exploitation.

Researchers Detail DifyTap Flaws in Dify That Could Expose AI Chats Across Tenants

The Hacker News
2026-06-22 5 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of four vulnerabilities in Dify, an open-source agentic workflow platform with more than 146,000 GitHub stars, that could allow attackers to stealthily read artificial intelligence (AI) conversions from other customers' applications without requiring authentication. The vulnerabilities have been collectively codenamed DifyTap by Zafran Security.

Dify cross-tenant file-preview UUID enumeration (CVE-2026-41949) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a single Dify console account/IP requesting the file-preview endpoint /console/api/files/{uuid}/preview for many distinct file UUIDs in a short window — the exact pattern of harvesting other tenants' uploaded documents (3,000 chars each) using only the file UUID. Article-specific because the vulnerable endpoint path and the UUID-keyed enumeration behaviour are the named exploit primitive. Rationale: Pivots on the exact vulnerable path '/console/api/files/{uuid}/preview' (confirmed by VulnCheck advisory and Dify 1.14.2 'tenant-scope FilePreviewApi text-extract' fix) and the distinct-UUID fan-out that is the only way to mass-harvest cross-tenant documents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/dify-authorization-bypass-via-file-preview-endpoint • https://github.com/langgenius/dify/releases/tag/1.14.2 • https://www.zafran.io/resources/difytap-zafran-discovers-how-attackers-can-silently-wiretap-ai-data-across-tenants-on-a-platform-powering-1m-apps
ATT&CKT1213 T1530
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Dify workspace admin doing bulk dataset cleanup, previewing many of their own uploaded documents
  • Automated re-embedding / dataset re-index job iterating files through an authenticated console session
  • Internal QA or load testing hammering the preview endpoint
  • A genuinely large knowledge-base where a power user browses dozens of documents in one sitting
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in ("dify-indexer-svc","dify-admin-automation") and SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8 internal automation hosts here")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the file UUID set for the flagged SourceUserName/SourceIP and confirm whether the IDs span multiple workspaces/tenants (cross-tenant = true positive). Check whether the account is an editor/standard user with no business reason to read these files. 2) Contain: disable the offending Dify console account and invalidate its sessions/tokens; if Dify is < 1.14.2, treat all previewed documents as exposed and prioritise upgrade. 3) Hunt: from the same SourceIP/account look for hits on /console/api/apps/*/trace (trace hijack) and plugin path-traversal requests; review what documents were exposed for sensitive data.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL has "/console/api/files/" and RequestURL has "/preview"
| extend FileId = extract(@"/console/api/files/([^/]+)/preview", 1, RequestURL)
| where isnotempty(FileId)
| summarize DistinctFileIds = dcount(FileId), Requests = count(), SampleFiles = make_set(FileId, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UAs = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 5) by SourceIP, SourceUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctFileIds >= 15   // 15 distinct file UUIDs / 10m on the preview endpoint = enumeration, not browsing
| order by DistinctFileIds desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| sort - distinct_file_ids
| tstats summariesonly=false count as preview_hits, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_file_ids, values(Web.uri_path) as paths from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/console/api/files/*/preview" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=10m

Dify Plugin Daemon path traversal to internal REST API (CVE-2026-41948) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts path-traversal sequences in requests routed to Dify's Plugin Daemon proxy — the unpatched (at disclosure) flaw where insufficient URL sanitization lets an authenticated user reach internal/private daemon endpoints and other tenants' plugin resources via GET/POST. Article-specific because it pairs the plugin-proxy path with traversal tokens rather than matching generic '../'. Rationale: Combines the Plugin Daemon proxy path keyword with literal and URL-encoded traversal tokens (matching the 'insufficient URL path sanitization' primitive described by Zafran/VulnCheck). Scoping to 'plugin' paths keeps it far tighter than a generic traversal rule; this CVE was still unpatched at disclosure so live exploitation is plausible. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/dify-authorization-bypass-via-trace-configuration-endpoints • https://securityaffairs.com/194081/hacking/difytap-four-bugs-put-over-1-million-ai-apps-at-risk.html • https://github.com/langgenius/dify/releases/tag/1.14.2

Data sourcesWeb

  • Security scanners (Nessus/Burp/ZAP) probing the Dify deployment with traversal payloads
  • Legitimate plugin names or query strings that incidentally contain '..' substrings
  • Penetration test or red-team engagement against the Dify host
  • Proxy that already URL-decodes and normalises paths, occasionally logging benign encoded sequences
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<authorised scanner IPs as a watchlist>") and RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request reached the Dify app (HTTP 200/302 vs WAF 403) and identify the authenticated SourceUserName; decode the traversal target to see which internal daemon endpoint was reached. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, disable the account, and apply the Dify GitHub build that fixes CVE-2026-41948 (not in 1.14.2). 3) Hunt: review the same actor for file-preview enumeration and trace-config writes, and check Plugin Daemon logs for cross-tenant plugin-icon/resource fetches.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL has "plugin"
| where RequestURL has_any ("../", "..%2f", "..%2F", "%2e%2e/", "%2e%2e%2f", "%2e%2e%2F", "..\\", "..%5c")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Dify mass trace-config hijack across apps (CVE-2026-41947) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a single Dify account/IP POSTing tracing configuration to many distinct application IDs (/console/api/apps/{app_id}/trace) — the persistent cross-tenant exfiltration channel where an attacker redirects all future chat messages/responses of victim apps to an attacker-controlled LLM trace provider. Article-specific because it keys on the trace-config endpoint plus the app-ID fan-out unique to this 'wiretap' technique. Rationale: Targets the named trace-config endpoint (confirmed by VulnCheck 'trace configuration endpoints' advisory and the Dify 1.14.2 'enforce tenant scoping on app trace-config endpoints' fix) and the app-ID fan-out that turns a single bug into an org-wide persistent exfil channel for AI chats. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/dify-authorization-bypass-via-trace-configuration-endpoints • https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/difytap-bugs-wiretap-ai-chat-histories • https://github.com/langgenius/dify/releases/tag/1.14.2
ATT&CKT1567 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A platform/MLOps engineer legitimately onboarding tracing (Langfuse/LangSmith/Opik) across many of their own apps in one session
  • Infrastructure-as-code or CI job that programmatically sets trace config for a fleet of apps
  • Migration to a new observability provider touching all workspace apps
  • A managed-service admin configuring tracing on behalf of multiple tenant apps they legitimately own
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in ("mlops-tracing-svc","dify-iac-bot")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the AppIds the account enabled tracing on and verify they belong to that user's own tenant/workspace; cross-tenant app_ids confirm hijack. Inspect the configured trace provider endpoint/host for an attacker-controlled or unfamiliar domain. 2) Contain: delete/disable the rogue trace configurations, suspend the account, and rotate any API/session tokens; upgrade to Dify 1.14.2 which scopes trace-config to tenant. 3) Hunt: pivot on the trace-provider destination domain across egress logs to scope data already exfiltrated, and correlate the same actor with file-preview enumeration and plugin traversal activity.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/console/api/apps/" and RequestURL has "/trace"
| extend AppId = extract(@"/console/api/apps/([^/]+)/trace", 1, RequestURL)
| where isnotempty(AppId)
| summarize DistinctApps = dcount(AppId), Posts = count(), SampleApps = make_set(AppId, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, SourceUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctApps >= 5   // one account enabling tracing on 5+ distinct apps/hr = mass wiretap, not normal config
| order by DistinctApps desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| tstats summariesonly=false count as trace_posts, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_apps, values(Web.uri_path) as app_paths from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.uri_path="/console/api/apps/*/trace*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=1h

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] SharePoint LFI recon via win.ini / web.config requests (Storm-2603 ToolShell precursor) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Velociraptor deployed with SYSTEM privileges (Storm-2603 LOTL tooling) · [LLM] BYOVD vulnerable-driver load to disable endpoint protection (Storm-2603 NSecKrnl/ServiceMouse) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Cloudflared tunnel established for covert C2 (Storm-2603) · [LLM] Visual Studio Code remote tunnel abused as SSH/C2 channel (Storm-2603) · [LLM] Zoho Assist unsanctioned remote-support agent on server (Storm-2603) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
SharePoint LFI recon via win.ini / web.config requests (Storm-2603 ToolShell precursor) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to internet-facing SharePoint/IIS servers that reference win.ini or web.config, the local-file-inclusion probe pattern DART observed Storm-2603 using to validate entry points before SharePoint ToolShell exploitation. Article-specific: it targets the exact recon filenames called out by DART rather than generic web scanning. Rationale: Uses DART's stated recon filenames win.ini and web.config against IIS/SharePoint logs; Defender Advanced Hunting has no IIS web-log table so defender_kql is intentionally empty and the detection runs on W3CIISLog / Web datamodel. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0058/
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing the SharePoint farm
  • Internal pen-test or red-team engagement against the same server
  • SharePoint admin downloading a backup web.config over HTTP
  • DR tooling fetching configuration files via web endpoints
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's full request history; is it external, geographically anomalous, and hitting /_layouts/ or /_vti_ paths around the same time? Check scStatus for 200 vs 404. 2) Contain: if external and unexpected, block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter and confirm SharePoint is patched for ToolShell (CVE-2025-49704/49706/53770/53771). 3) Hunt: search the same host for w3wp.exe spawning cmd/powershell, dropped .aspx web shells under TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS, and subsequent Velociraptor/cloudflared execution.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("win.ini","web.config") or csUriQuery has_any ("win.ini","web.config")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Velociraptor deployed with SYSTEM privileges (Storm-2603 LOTL tooling) AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the Velociraptor forensic agent, which DART observed Storm-2603 deploying at SYSTEM to map the environment under the cover of legitimate IR tooling. Catches renamed binaries via product/description metadata and flags elevated or config-driven invocations. Rationale: Velociraptor is named explicitly by DART as Storm-2603's mapping tool run at SYSTEM; matching on the binary plus product metadata catches renames, and the integrity-level / --config clauses raise fidelity. Corroborated by Huntress' Velociraptor-misuse research tying it to the same actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0058/
ATT&CKT1219 T1588.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Org's own DFIR/IR team legitimately running Velociraptor during an investigation
  • MSSP onboarding Velociraptor as a sanctioned EDR/hunt agent
  • Security training lab or tabletop exercise
  • Threat-hunting POC evaluating Velociraptor
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether your IR team sanctioned Velociraptor on this host; check the binary's path (Temp/Public = suspicious), SHA256 reputation, and parent process (w3wp.exe parent = SharePoint exploitation). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the process, and capture the --config file (reveals attacker C2/frontend). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for cloudflared tunnels, VS Code 'code tunnel', Zoho Assist, new admin accounts, and the NSecKrnl.sys/AToolsKrnl64.sys drivers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "velociraptor.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Velociraptor" or ProcessVersionInfoFileDescription has "Velociraptor"
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in ("System","High") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--config","artifacts collect","gui","frontend","client")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\velociraptor.exe" or CommandLine has "velociraptor"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloudflared tunnel established for covert C2 (Storm-2603) AICommand & Control High
Detects execution of cloudflared with tunnel arguments or use of trycloudflare.com, one of the multiple remote-access channels DART attributes to Storm-2603 for persistent egress. Highly anomalous on a SharePoint/IIS server. Rationale: cloudflared + tunnel/trycloudflare is a Storm-2603 remote-access channel named by DART; pairing the binary with tunnel arguments keeps FPs near zero, especially on server roles where cloudflared has no business running. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using Cloudflare Tunnel to expose an internal dev app
  • DevOps publishing a service via cloudflared as sanctioned infra
  • Cloudflare Zero Trust connector deployed by IT
  • QA testing a trycloudflare quick tunnel
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the tunnel target/token from the command line and the host role; cloudflared on a SharePoint/DC is a strong TP signal. 2) Contain: kill cloudflared, block *.trycloudflare.com and Cloudflare tunnel egress at the firewall, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: enumerate other egress channels on the host (Zoho Assist, VS Code tunnel, SSH), review new local/domain admin accounts created in the same window, and check for Velociraptor.

Visual Studio Code remote tunnel abused as SSH/C2 channel (Storm-2603) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects 'code tunnel' / code-tunnel.exe execution, which Storm-2603 used to stand up SSH-based command-and-control through VS Code's dev-tunnel service. On a server this is a high-fidelity C2 indicator, not developer activity. Rationale: DART names SSH-via-VS-Code as a Storm-2603 remote-access channel; 'code tunnel' is the exact CLI that stands up a dev-tunnel C2, and on server roles it has effectively no legitimate use. Network pivot is *.devtunnels.ms / tunnels.api.visualstudio.com. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm
ATT&CKT1572 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstation legitimately using VS Code Remote Tunnels
  • Engineer remoting into a build/jump host via code tunnel
  • Sanctioned remote-dev workflow on a dev server
  • CI agent invoking VS Code CLI
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check host role (server vs dev endpoint) and account; correlate outbound connections to *.devtunnels.ms / global.rel.tunnels.api.visualstudio.com. 2) Contain: kill the tunnel process, revoke the associated GitHub/Microsoft tunnel auth, block dev-tunnel domains on servers, isolate if on a server role. 3) Hunt: look for cloudflared, Zoho Assist, Velociraptor and newly created admin accounts on the same host/account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName =~ "code.exe" or FileName =~ "code-tunnel.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Visual Studio Code")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\code.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\code-tunnel.exe")
| where CommandLine has "tunnel"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BYOVD vulnerable-driver load to disable endpoint protection (Storm-2603 NSecKrnl/ServiceMouse) AIInstallation High
Detects the write or service-install of the vulnerable kernel drivers Storm-2603 used for memory tampering and disabling defenses — NSecKrnl.sys (DART report) and the Antiy-derived AToolsKrnl64.sys loaded via the ServiceMouse service (earlier Storm-2603 ops). Each is a named, high-fidelity BYOVD artifact. Rationale: Drives off the exact BYOVD driver names attributed to Storm-2603 — NSecKrnl.sys from the DART report and AToolsKrnl64.sys + the ServiceMouse service from Check Point's prior Storm-2603 analysis — making both file-write and service-install variants near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/storm-2603-deploys-custom-malware-using-byovd/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/before-toolshell-exploring-storm-2603s-previous-ransomware-operations/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1543.003 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Antiy Labs AV legitimately installed (uses AToolsKrnl64.sys) on an endpoint
  • Vendor security software shipping a same-named signed driver
  • Driver-research/sandbox VM intentionally loading vulnerable drivers
  • Forensic imaging of an already-compromised disk re-surfacing the artifact
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe") or FolderPath has @"\Temp\" or FolderPath has @"\Public\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Antiy AV is a sanctioned product in the estate; check the writing process, signer, and SHA256 of the .sys against the known-vulnerable hashes, and whether a ServiceMouse service was created. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop/delete the ServiceMouse service, block the driver hash, and treat EDR telemetry from this host as potentially blinded. 3) Hunt: review for IOCTL-driven process kills of AV/EDR, preceding SharePoint exploitation, Velociraptor, and ransomware staging on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("NSecKrnl.sys","AToolsKrnl64.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceName =~ "ServiceMouse" or ServiceFileName has_any ("NSecKrnl.sys","AToolsKrnl64.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zoho Assist unsanctioned remote-support agent on server (Storm-2603) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts execution of Zoho Assist remote-support binaries, one of the parallel remote-access channels DART attributes to Storm-2603 for persistence. On SharePoint/server roles where no help-desk uses Zoho, this is a strong unauthorized-RMM signal. Rationale: Zoho Assist is named by DART as a Storm-2603 remote-access channel; matching the company metadata plus the known agent binaries flags unsanctioned RMM, which is most damning on server roles with no help-desk Zoho usage. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT help desk that legitimately uses Zoho Assist for endpoint support
  • MSP managing the estate via Zoho RMM
  • User-initiated Zoho support session for a software issue
  • Sanctioned Zoho ManageEngine deployment
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Zoho Assist is an approved tool and whether this host/account should have it; server roles and SharePoint hosts are high-signal. 2) Contain: terminate the agent, uninstall, block Zoho Assist gateway domains for server VLANs, and isolate if unauthorized. 3) Hunt: correlate with cloudflared, VS Code tunnel, Velociraptor, the BYOVD drivers, and new admin accounts created in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Zoho" or FileName has_any ("ZohoURS","ZA_Connect","ZA_Access","ZMAgent") or ProcessCommandLine has "Zoho Assist"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ZohoURS","ZA_Connect","ZA_Access","ZMAgent") or CommandLine has "Zoho Assist"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423") or SHA1 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423") or MD5 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423") or SHA1 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423") or MD5 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New OXLOADER Loader Uses Malicious Google Ads to Deliver CastleStealer

The Hacker News
2026-06-22 11 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new campaign that delivers CastleStealer by means of a previously unreported malware loader dubbed OXLOADER. According to Elastic Security Labs, the campaign leverages malicious Google Ads as a starting point to distribute the malware. Evidence indicates that the threat actor is likely Russian-speaking and financially motivated, owing to the

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] REF8372 malvertising delivery domains (prentiva99.info / miloyannopoulos.com) contacted · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New OXLOADER Loader Uses Malicious Google Ads to Deliver CastleStealer
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OXLOADER fake-installer batch spawns PowerShell -Verb RunAs to fetch Storj payload · [LLM] OXLOADER DLL side-load: Windows dui70.dll loaded from a non-system path · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CastleStealer C2 beacon to 89.124.95.161 / 89.124.115.82 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
REF8372 malvertising delivery domains (prentiva99.info / miloyannopoulos.com) contacted AIDelivery High
Hunts host connections or DNS lookups to the OXLOADER campaign's fake Node.js landing page and 302 redirector that fronts the Storj-hosted payload. These are dedicated attacker domains, so any hit is a near-certain compromise of the delivery stage. Rationale: Both domains are dedicated to the campaign per Elastic Security Labs (node-js.prentiva99.info landing page, app.miloyannopoulos.com 302 redirector to the Storj payload); they appear nowhere in legitimate traffic, making any hit high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/oxloader-malware-loader-infostealer • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-oxloader-loader-uses-malicious.html

  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample from the corporate range
  • Threat-intel crawler / URL scanner resolving the IOC domains
  • Proxy prefetch or browser DNS-prefetch of a link in a TI report email
  • Internal blocklist test traffic generated by the SOC itself

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which host/user resolved the domain and whether a browser search for 'node.js'/'lts node' preceded it; pull the answering IP and any subsequent Storj connection. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block prentiva99.info / miloyannopoulos.com and *.storjshare.io raw paths at the proxy/DNS, and disable the user's session pending review. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (cmd→powershell -Verb RunAs Storj download) and UC3 (dui70.dll side-load) on the same host, and sweep the org for other resolvers of these domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("prentiva99.info","miloyannopoulos.com")
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("BATPackageBuilderSetup.bat","BATPackageBulderSetup.bat","aBsvwbdas.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("prentiva99.info","miloyannopoulos.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResolvedIPs = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OXLOADER fake-installer batch spawns PowerShell -Verb RunAs to fetch Storj payload AIInstallation High
Hunts the OXLOADER staging step where BATPackageBuilderSetup.bat runs a PowerShell command that downloads aBsvwbdas.exe from link.storjshare.io and relaunches it with -Verb RunAs to trigger a UAC elevation prompt. The combination of PowerShell elevation plus a Storj raw-download string is unique to this fake installer chain. Rationale: Elastic confirms BATPackageBuilderSetup.bat (and typo variant BATPackageBulderSetup.bat) downloads aBsvwbdas.exe from link.storjshare.io and re-runs it with -Verb RunAs; pairing PowerShell elevation with the Storj raw-host/filename strings is specific to this fake-installer chain and avoids generic encoded-PowerShell rules. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/oxloader-malware-loader-infostealer
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1548.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin packaging script that legitimately uses Start-Process -Verb RunAs (won't match without the Storj/filename string)
  • Developer manually downloading a build artifact from link.storjshare.io
  • RMM/software-deployment tool elevating a vendor installer from a CDN (non-Storj, filtered)
  • Red-team replication of the OXLOADER chain in a test range
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("nodejs.org","npmjs.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent is cmd.exe running a *Setup*.bat from a user-writable path (Downloads/Temp) and capture the full PowerShell line and the Storj URL; check whether a UAC prompt was accepted. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the powershell and aBsvwbdas.exe processes, and quarantine the dropped .bat/.exe by hash. 3) Hunt: search the same host for dui70.dll side-loading (UC3) and CastleStealer C2 (UC4), and sweep the org for any execution of the campaign SHA-256s.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "RunAs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("storjshare.io","aBsvwbdas.exe","BATPackageBuilderSetup","BATPackageBulderSetup")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has "RunAs"
| where CommandLine has_any ("storjshare.io","aBsvwbdas.exe","BATPackageBuilderSetup","BATPackageBulderSetup")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OXLOADER DLL side-load: Windows dui70.dll loaded from a non-system path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OXLOADER execution stage where a copy of the Windows DirectUI Engine DLL (dui70.dll) is loaded from outside System32/WinSxS — the signed-binary cover OXLOADER abuses to map and decrypt CastleStealer via a new RWX .xtext section. Also covers direct execution of the two known OXLOADER masquerade hashes. Rationale: Elastic identifies dui70.dll as the legitimate signed DLL OXLOADER side-loads (creating an RWX .xtext section to decrypt CastleStealer); a System32 DLL loading from any other path is anomalous, and the two OXLOADER masquerade SHA-256s give a hard hash fallback on Falcon. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/oxloader-malware-loader-infostealer
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A portable/third-party app that bundles its own copy of dui70.dll in its install directory
  • WinSxS servicing or in-place upgrade staging dui70.dll under a temp servicing path
  • Developer debugging environment loading a redistributed UI DLL
  • EDR/forensic tooling rehydrating the DLL during analysis
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that loaded the non-system dui70.dll, its folder, and signer; check for a sibling randomly-named .ocx and a section named .xtext in the loader image. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader process, and quarantine the loader EXE plus the dropped DLL/.ocx by hash. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the UC2 batch/PowerShell chain and forward to UC4 CastleStealer C2 (89.124.95.161 / 89.124.115.82) on the same host; block the OXLOADER hashes org-wide.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "dui70.dll"
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\") and not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\WinSxS\") and not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\SysWOW64\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedFrom = FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceImageLoadEvents

| where FileName =~ "dui70.dll"

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedFrom = FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CastleStealer C2 beacon to 89.124.95.161 / 89.124.115.82 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the two CastleStealer command-and-control IPs delivered by OXLOADER in REF8372. As dedicated stealer C2 endpoints, any host reaching them indicates a completed infection exfiltrating browser/credential data. Rationale: Elastic lists 89.124.95.161 and 89.124.115.82 as CastleStealer C2 servers for this campaign; matching destination IP is a direct, high-fidelity post-infection signal and surfaces the initiating process so the analyst can pivot to the loader without hand-editing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/oxloader-malware-loader-infostealer
ATT&CKT1071 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The hosting IP is later reassigned to a benign service (re-validate IP age before alerting weeks out)
  • SOC threat-intel scanner or honeypot deliberately probing the C2 IP
  • Researcher detonating the sample in a monitored VM on the corporate network
  • Shared-hosting neighbor on the same /24 serving unrelated legitimate content
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process initiating the connection (expect the OXLOADER-spawned binary or a side-loaded host process), confirm the host previously walked UC1/UC2, and capture port/protocol and bytes out. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 89.124.95.161 and 89.124.115.82 at the firewall/proxy, and force-reset credentials for any account used on the host (CastleStealer harvests browser/credential data). 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to both IPs and for the campaign hashes; review what secrets/sessions the user held for targeted rotation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("89.124.95.161","89.124.115.82")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("89.124.95.161","89.124.115.82")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

SecurityEvent

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37", "de4f51649ec1a33071854aefe93ffb3fc225e19f802d8dd914676dd5dfef2615", "9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d", "c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe", "4ec9d9d4d10ad78fc6d7bda7cb17d52984878ccd2dd4302fd1cef152313b9741", "39019279686c820c3af5684012a0085a7e2109f612c9fab886dd0577ace5b5c6") or SHA1 in~ ("fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37", "de4f51649ec1a33071854aefe93ffb3fc225e19f802d8dd914676dd5dfef2615", "9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d", "c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe", "4ec9d9d4d10ad78fc6d7bda7cb17d52984878ccd2dd4302fd1cef152313b9741", "39019279686c820c3af5684012a0085a7e2109f612c9fab886dd0577ace5b5c6") or MD5 in~ ("fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37", "de4f51649ec1a33071854aefe93ffb3fc225e19f802d8dd914676dd5dfef2615", "9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d", "c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe", "4ec9d9d4d10ad78fc6d7bda7cb17d52984878ccd2dd4302fd1cef152313b9741", "39019279686c820c3af5684012a0085a7e2109f612c9fab886dd0577ace5b5c6")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37", "de4f51649ec1a33071854aefe93ffb3fc225e19f802d8dd914676dd5dfef2615", "9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d", "c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe", "4ec9d9d4d10ad78fc6d7bda7cb17d52984878ccd2dd4302fd1cef152313b9741", "39019279686c820c3af5684012a0085a7e2109f612c9fab886dd0577ace5b5c6") or SHA1 in~ ("fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37", "de4f51649ec1a33071854aefe93ffb3fc225e19f802d8dd914676dd5dfef2615", "9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d", "c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe", "4ec9d9d4d10ad78fc6d7bda7cb17d52984878ccd2dd4302fd1cef152313b9741", "39019279686c820c3af5684012a0085a7e2109f612c9fab886dd0577ace5b5c6") or MD5 in~ ("fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37", "de4f51649ec1a33071854aefe93ffb3fc225e19f802d8dd914676dd5dfef2615", "9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d", "c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe", "4ec9d9d4d10ad78fc6d7bda7cb17d52984878ccd2dd4302fd1cef152313b9741", "39019279686c820c3af5684012a0085a7e2109f612c9fab886dd0577ace5b5c6")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fdfc7831e5c24cfa80152860dfe8c056ba079f7df1393bf6bb7b18ed974eda37", "de4f51649ec1a33071854aefe93ffb3fc225e19f802d8dd914676dd5dfef2615", "9a9939dff297997732aaade9b243d695632cbd64033c5fbcb9de3d09b7e6c28d", "c85f2765a6c3c3f3907c17e57df12f8f68826f74bff3bbfd272af50666d065fe", "4ec9d9d4d10ad78fc6d7bda7cb17d52984878ccd2dd4302fd1cef152313b9741", "39019279686c820c3af5684012a0085a7e2109f612c9fab886dd0577ace5b5c6"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

A VBScript campaign distributed through WhatsApp deploying RMM software

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-22 14 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] WhatsApp Desktop spawning WScript executing VBS from attachment Transfers dir · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] UAC ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin disabled (set to 0) by Windows Script Host · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — A VBScript campaign distributed through WhatsApp deploying RMM software
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] VBScript creating hidden working directory and VBS payloads under C:\Users\Public\Documents · [LLM] Renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe running from Public\Documents working directory · [LLM] ManageEngine Endpoint Central (UEMS) agent silently installed as final RMM payload · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Beacon/download to WhatsApp-VBS campaign C2 infrastructure (202.61.160.0/24 + 38.55.151.63) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
WhatsApp Desktop spawning WScript executing VBS from attachment Transfers dir AIDelivery High
Hunts the campaign's initial-access foothold: WScript.exe launched directly by WhatsApp Desktop (WhatsApp.Root.exe) or executing a .vbs/.vbe from the WhatsApp UWP package Transfers path. This is the exact process relationship Kaspersky documented confirming the financial-lure VBScript was run from the WhatsApp client. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim WhatsApp UWP package path (5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\...\Transfers) and parent WhatsApp.Root.exe from the article's process-tree analysis plus the .vbs/.vbe extension - a combination no benign workflow produces. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-uncovers-a-new-massive-campaign-spreading-malware-via-whatsapp
ATT&CKT1566 T1204.002 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate .vbs business automation a user genuinely received and ran via WhatsApp (rare in enterprise but possible in some SME workflows)
  • Security testing / red-team simulation of WhatsApp-delivered scripts
  • A user manually saving then double-clicking a benign VBS from chat (parent would be explorer.exe, not WhatsApp.Root.exe - reduces FP)
  • EDR/AV sandbox detonation of submitted samples on an analyst workstation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("devenv.exe","sense.exe") // exclude EDR sandbox/dev detonation hosts; tune to your analyst VLAN device group
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 of the VBS; check the file name against the campaign's financial-lure list (Financial Reports.vbs, Account Statement.vbs, Debt Statement.vbs, etc.) and look for the child wscript downloading to C:\Users\Public\Documents\. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the wscript.exe tree, and quarantine the VBS from the WhatsApp Transfers folder; reset the sending contact's WhatsApp session (account likely compromised). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same DeviceId for the working-dir creation under Public\Documents, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0 registry write, and outbound connections to 202.61.160.0/24 / 38.55.151.63.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "WhatsApp.Root.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs", ".vbe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "cscript.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "WhatsApp.Root.exe"
    or CommandLine has @"\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\"
| where CommandLine has_any (".vbs", ".vbe")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WhatsApp Desktop Spawning WScript Executing VBS Attachment
id: 6f3c1a2e-9b54-4f7d-8c21-2a1d6e0b4f10
description: Detects WScript/CScript launched by WhatsApp Desktop or executing a VBS/VBE from the WhatsApp UWP package Transfers directory, matching the WhatsApp VBScript RMM campaign.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  selection_parent_or_path:
    - ParentImage|endswith: '\WhatsApp.Root.exe'
    - CommandLine|contains: '\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\'
  selection_ext:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.vbs'
      - '.vbe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_parent_or_path and selection_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) (@ParentImage:(*\\WhatsApp.Root.exe OR *\\whatsapp.root.exe) OR @CommandLine:*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*) @CommandLine:(*.vbs* OR *.vbe*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| (ParentBaseFileName=/whatsapp\.root\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/\\Packages\\5319275A\.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\/i)
| CommandLine=/\.(vbs|vbe)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=wscript.exe OR Processes.process_name=cscript.exe) AND (Processes.parent_process_name="WhatsApp.Root.exe" OR Processes.process="*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*") AND (Processes.process="*.vbs*" OR Processes.process="*.vbe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=wscript.exe OR Processes.process_name=cscript.exe) AND (Processes.parent_process_name="WhatsApp.Root.exe" OR Processes.process="*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*") AND (Processes.process="*.vbs*" OR Processes.process="*.vbe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
VBScript creating hidden working directory and VBS payloads under C:\Users\Public\Documents AIInstallation High
Hunts Stage 1 staging: WScript/CScript writing files into a randomized Temp_<random> or MSUpdate_<random> working directory under C:\Users\Public\Documents\, often flagged hidden+system. This is the campaign's payload-staging step prior to fetching the two secondary VBS scripts. Rationale: Uses the verbatim staging path C:\Users\Public\Documents\ plus the two documented randomized directory prefixes Temp_ and MSUpdate_, scoped to a wscript/cscript writer - benign software almost never drops VBS into Public\Documents under those name patterns. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that legitimately stage VBS helpers in Public\Documents (uncommon, but check vendor)
  • IT logon-script tooling writing temp VBS to a shared public path
  • Backup/imaging software that names temp folders Temp_<id> (would not be a wscript writer - excluded by process filter)
  • Software installers using Public\Documents as a shared scratch area
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Veeam\", @"\Backup\")) // drop known backup scratch paths if they surface
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Enumerate the contents of the flagged Public\Documents working directory; capture any .vbs/.vbe and check for renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe (DLL-like names) inside it. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, delete/quarantine the working directory, and kill the parent wscript tree. 3) HUNT: Tie the same DeviceId back to a WhatsApp.Root.exe -> wscript launch (UC1) and forward to ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin registry change and 202.61.160.0/24 egress.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_") or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".vbe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_") or TargetFileExtension in~ ("vbs","vbe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe running from Public\Documents working directory AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's LOLBin masquerading: curl.exe or bitsadmin.exe copied into the working directory and renamed with DLL-like filenames, exposed via the OriginalFileName-vs-FileName mismatch while executing from C:\Users\Public\Documents\. Used to download the secondary VBS payloads and the RMM ZIP. Rationale: Pivots on the article's documented trick of copying curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe under DLL-like names in the working dir - the PE OriginalFileName stays curl/bitsadmin while the on-disk FileName differs, a near-zero-FP masquerade signal when scoped to Public\Documents. Sentinel falls back to path+download-flag heuristics since 4688 lacks OriginalFileName. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
ATT&CKT1036.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or admin manually copying curl.exe to a scratch dir and renaming it for testing
  • Portable-app launchers that bundle a renamed curl.exe
  • Software updaters shipping curl under a vendor-specific name (rarely in Public\Documents)
  • Sysmon OriginalFileName field unpopulated on very old binaries (causes misses, not FPs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") // only keep LOLBins launched by the script host, dropping dev/admin manual copies
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the renamed binary's hash and full command line - extract the download URL it fetched (compare against 202.61.160.0/24, 38.55.151.63, baoxis.cc). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, quarantine the renamed LOLBin and any downloaded ZIP/VBS in the working dir. 3) HUNT: Look on the same host for the resulting UEMSAgent.msi/.mst install and the ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin registry write; sweep org for other hosts running curl/bitsadmin from Public\Documents.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName in~ ("curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where FileName !in~ ("curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_")
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://", "https://", "--url", "/transfer", "-o ", "--output")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
