| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.original_file_name=curl.exe OR Processes.original_file_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND NOT (Processes.process_name=curl.exe OR Processes.process_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.original_file_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

UAC ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin disabled (set to 0) by Windows Script Host AIExploitation High
Detects the Stage 2 'VBS script 1' behaviour: a script-host process writing HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin (or EnableLUA) to 0 to suppress admin elevation prompts. Scoped to wscript/cscript or a Public\Documents writer so it isolates the campaign's UAC-weakening step. Rationale: Uses the exact registry path from the article's Table 2 (HKLM\...\Policies\System\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin) corroborated by SOCRadar's note that the value is set to 0, scoped to a script-host writer so legitimate GPO/admin UAC changes are excluded. Falcon left blank: UAC policy value is not an ASEP and is not reliably carried in AsepValueUpdate FDR telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
ATT&CKT1548.002 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GPO or Intune policy lowering UAC (initiating process would be svchost/gpsvc, not wscript - excluded)
  • Admin manually disabling UAC via a configuration script
  • Vendor installers that toggle UAC during setup (rare, and not script-host-driven)
  • Security baseline rollback tooling
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","svchost.exe","taskhostw.exe") // exclude policy-driven UAC changes
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writer is wscript/cscript and correlate with a Public\Documents working dir on the same host; re-enable UAC immediately (set ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin back to 5, EnableLUA to 1). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, kill the script tree, and treat the host as elevated-compromise. 3) HUNT: Look for the follow-on UEMSAgent RMM install and any repeated ShellExecute runas elevation loops; sweep for the same registry write across the estate.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin","EnableLUA")
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Policies\System"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin","EnableLUA")
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beacon/download to WhatsApp-VBS campaign C2 infrastructure (202.61.160.0/24 + 38.55.151.63) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects host connections to the campaign's attacker-controlled UEMS/management-server IPs and download domains. Confirmed by SOCRadar; the 202.61.160.x range overlaps prior ValleyRAT/Gh0st RAT infrastructure. Fires on any endpoint reaching these IOCs, with the initiating process surfaced for triage. Rationale: All six IPs are second-source-confirmed (SOCRadar lists the same 202.61.160.x management-server set plus 38.55.151.63, with 202.61.160.201 tied to prior ValleyRAT/Gh0st RAT infra). Domains are kept as has_any enrichment from the article's IOC list. CIDR 202.61.160.0/24 covers all five .160 hosts in one clause. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://www.technadu.com/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-installs-manageengine-rmm-kaspersky-warns/629801/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher/analyst sandbox deliberately reaching the IOCs for study
  • Threat-intel scanning or proxy that proactively resolves IOC domains
  • Shared hosting reuse - 202.61.160.0/24 belongs to a provider that may also host benign sites (validate the exact host)
  • Legitimate use of oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com (Alibaba OSS) by unrelated apps - validate the full sdcwww subdomain before alerting on the domain clause
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in ("202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63") // keep all IP hits; drop only browser hits to the shared-hosting Aliyun domain
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process - if it is wscript.exe, msiexec.exe, or a renamed curl/bitsadmin from Public\Documents, treat as confirmed; capture URL/port and bytes transferred. 2) CONTAIN: Block the IPs (and 202.61.160.0/24) and domains at the egress proxy/firewall, isolate the host. 3) HUNT: Pivot to the host's process tree for the WhatsApp->wscript chain, the UEMS RMM install, and the UAC registry change; sweep all hosts that resolved the IOC domains.
let c2ips = dynamic(["202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63"]);
let c2domains = dynamic(["temu.baskwms.top","invoice.msopsa.top","baoxis.cc","sdcwww.oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2ips = dynamic(["202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63"]);
let c2domains = dynamic(["temu.baskwms.top","invoice.msopsa.top","baoxis.cc","sdcwww.oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (c2ips) or Url has_any (c2domains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ManageEngine Endpoint Central (UEMS) agent silently installed as final RMM payload AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's end goal: deployment of a preconfigured ManageEngine Endpoint Central agent (UEMSAgent.msi + attacker UEMSAgent.mst transform + DCAgentServerInfo.json) giving covert remote access. Scoped to script-host / Public\Documents-spawned installs so it isolates abuse from legitimate enterprise Endpoint Central rollouts. Rationale: Anchors on the exact RMM artifact names UEMSAgent.msi, the attacker UEMSAgent.mst transform, and DCAgentServerInfo.json (ManageEngine Endpoint Central) confirmed by SOCRadar, gated on a script-host/Public\Documents context so legitimate sanctioned Endpoint Central deployments (pushed by your own server via SYSTEM/services) don't fire. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-uses-fake.html
ATT&CKT1219 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned ManageEngine Endpoint Central agent rollout by your IT team (initiating process would be the EC server push / SYSTEM service, not wscript - the context gate excludes it)
  • Endpoint Central self-update writing agent files under Program Files (not Public\Documents)
  • An admin manually staging UEMSAgent.msi in a downloads/temp folder for testing
  • MSP-managed devices where Endpoint Central is the legitimate RMM (validate the management server in DCAgentServerInfo.json against your known UEMS server)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dcagentregister.exe","dcagenttrayicon.exe","services.exe") // exclude legitimate Endpoint Central self-managed agent file writes
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open DCAgentServerInfo.json and the .mst transform - compare the configured management server against your sanctioned Endpoint Central server; if it points to 202.61.160.0/24 / 38.55.151.63 it is malicious. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, stop/uninstall the rogue UEMS agent and its service, kill active remote sessions, and block the management-server IPs. 3) HUNT: Trace back to the WhatsApp->wscript chain and UAC change on the host, and sweep the org for any UEMSAgent install whose server config is not your own.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("UEMSAgent.msi","UEMSAgent.mst","DCAgentServerInfo.json")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","msiexec.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
    or FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "UEMSAgent" or CommandLine has "DCAgentServerInfo"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "cscript.exe" or CommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

status: experimental

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or SHA1 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or MD5 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or SHA1 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or MD5 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AryStinger NAS recon tooling execution (fscan, ksubdomain, httpx, gs-netcat) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
AryStinger C2 / download infrastructure contact (ajb8.com, 107.150.106.14) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any monitored host resolving or connecting to AryStinger's hard-coded C2 and payload-staging infrastructure: the domain ajb8.com (and subhosts) and the original spreader IP 107.150.106.14. Catches both an infected on-prem Linux NAS Executor beaconing out and any internal host being footprinted from the proxy fleet's staging host. Rationale: ajb8.com and 107.150.106.14 are the two concrete network IOCs the article cites and XLab/SecurityAffairs/BleepingComputer corroborate; both are pure-IOC, so any resolution/connection is high-fidelity with near-zero benign overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://securityaffairs.com/193987/security/4300-outdated-routers-hijacked-in-stealthy-spy-infrastructure-by-arystinger-malware.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/arystinger-botnet-infected-thousands-of-d-link-routers-worldwide/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/arystinger-botnet-hijacks-4300-routers/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security analyst manually browsing the XLab IOC writeup that embeds the ajb8.com string in a URL/referrer (web-proxy log only, not actual resolution)
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox detonating an AryStinger sample and resolving ajb8.com from a controlled host
  • Internal DNS sinkhole already redirecting ajb8.com (the query still logs but answer is sinkhole IP)
  • Stale passive-DNS replay tooling re-resolving historical indicators
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and isnotempty(RemoteUrl))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying/connecting host and its OS — if it's a Linux NAS/router or an EOL D-Link/QNAP appliance, treat as likely-infected; pull the initiating process (Executor binary). 2) Contain: block ajb8.com and 107.150.106.14 at the egress firewall/DNS, isolate the device from the network, and snapshot it for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for /tmp/bin drops, syswapd0h/syswapd0w processes, dropbear on port 2332, and outbound DNS-scan volume; sweep other appliances for the same IOC set.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "ajb8.com" or RemoteIP == "107.150.106.14"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has "ajb8.com" | extend Host = Computer, SrcIP = ClientIP, Indicator = Name),
  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP == "107.150.106.14" or DestinationHostName has "ajb8.com" | extend Host = SourceHostName, SrcIP = SourceIP, Indicator = coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationIP))
| project TimeGenerated, Host, SrcIP, Indicator
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AryStinger Executor implant drop/exec in /tmp/bin (syswapd0h, syswapd0w) AIInstallation High
Hunts the AryStinger node implant on onboarded Linux hosts (e.g. compromised QNAP NAS): an ELF written to or executed from /tmp/bin, or a process masquerading as a swap daemon named syswapd0h / syswapd0w. These names mimic a legitimate system daemon but are unique to this campaign. Rationale: syswapd0h/syswapd0w are campaign-unique implant process names and /tmp/bin is the cited staging path — both are explicitly called out as the 'what to check' indicators and corroborated by HeroDevs/SecurityAffairs, giving very low benign overlap on a Linux appliance. Cross-checked against: • https://www.herodevs.com/blog-posts/arystinger-forgotten-routers-recon-proxy-network • https://securityaffairs.com/193987/security/4300-outdated-routers-hijacked-in-stealthy-spy-infrastructure-by-arystinger-malware.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin debugging tooling temporarily compiled/run from /tmp/bin on a build server
  • Package-manager or installer scratch binaries executed from /tmp on a CI host
  • Security researcher detonating an AryStinger sample on an onboarded sandbox VM
  • A genuinely-named swap helper from an obscure embedded distro (rare — verify hash against the implant)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/usr/lib" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a Linux NAS/appliance, capture the SHA256 of the /tmp/bin binary, and check VirusTotal/XLab IOC list — AryStinger's ELF was 0/VT at discovery so absence of detection is itself a signal. 2) Contain: kill the syswapd0h/syswapd0w process, isolate the host, and preserve /tmp/bin for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate to ajb8.com beaconing, dropbear listener on 2332, gs-netcat, and recon-tool (fscan/ksubdomain/httpx) execution on the same aid; sweep peer appliances.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("syswapd0h","syswapd0w") or FolderPath startswith "/tmp/bin"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

AryStinger Dropbear SSH persistence on hard-coded port 2332 AIInstallation High
Hunts AryStinger's router-side persistence: a Dropbear SSH server launched on the fixed, campaign-specific port 2332 (vs the standard 22). Detecting the dropbear binary invoked with -p 2332, or a new listener on TCP/2332, surfaces the persistence backdoor on onboarded Linux devices. Rationale: Port 2332 is the article's explicit hard-coded Dropbear persistence port; pairing the dropbear binary with the literal 2332 in cmdline is highly specific to this campaign and rare in legitimate SSH config. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/arystinger-botnet-hijacks-4300-routers/ • https://www.herodevs.com/blog-posts/arystinger-forgotten-routers-recon-proxy-network
ATT&CKT1571 T1021.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Ports
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin who legitimately runs Dropbear on a custom port that happens to include 2332 (e.g. an embedded device hardening standard)
  • IoT/OpenWrt firmware that ships Dropbear with a non-default port set by org policy
  • Network appliance test harness spinning up Dropbear listeners during QA
  • Penetration-test infrastructure deploying Dropbear backdoors during an authorised engagement
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Dropbear-on-2332 is an approved config for the host; check who/what spawned it (parent process — Executor implant vs init). 2) Contain: stop the dropbear service, block inbound TCP/2332 at the firewall, rotate any device credentials, and check authorized_keys for the hard-coded key fingerprint (sh_#@!_2024_secret). 3) Hunt: correlate with /tmp/bin implant, ajb8.com beaconing, and recon-tool execution on the same host; scan the estate for any device listening on 2332.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "dropbear" and ProcessCommandLine has "2332"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "dropbear" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "2332"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AryStinger NAS recon tooling execution (fscan, ksubdomain, httpx, gs-netcat) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the AryStinger Go NAS Executor's on-host reconnaissance: execution of fscan (port/service scanner), ksubdomain (subdomain enumeration), httpx (HTTP probing), or the gs-netcat persistence/tunneling tool on an onboarded Linux host. These offensive recon binaries running on a NAS/appliance — especially parented by /tmp/bin or a syswapd process — indicate the device is now a footprinting node. Rationale: fscan, ksubdomain, httpx and gs-netcat are the exact recon/tunneling tools the article names the Go Executor deploying; their presence on a NAS/appliance is article-specific, though httpx has some legit-tooling overlap so this stays hunting-tier with a parent-process filter. Cross-checked against: • https://www.techradar.com/pro/security/thousands-of-d-link-and-qnap-nas-routers-compromised-by-fast-moving-arystinger-malware-that-turns-unsecured-devices-into-a-malicious-proxy-botnet • https://cybersecuritynews.com/arystinger-botnet-hijacks-4300-routers/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security team running an authorised internal scan with fscan/httpx from a jump host
  • DevOps using ProjectDiscovery httpx legitimately in a CI/CD asset-inventory pipeline
  • A bug-bounty researcher's recon box that is also onboarded to EDR
  • Red-team engagement staging the same open-source tools
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/bin" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("syswapd0h","syswapd0w")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent process and path — recon tools parented by /tmp/bin or syswapd0h/syswapd0w on a NAS is malicious; from a sanctioned scanner host with a ticket it's benign. 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate the device, kill the Executor and child recon processes, and capture scan targets/output from the command lines. 3) Hunt: pivot to ajb8.com C2, /tmp/bin implant, dropbear on 2332, and review DNS-scan egress volume; identify which internal/external ranges were footprinted to scope downstream exposure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("fscan","ksubdomain","httpx","gs-netcat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("fscan","ksubdomain","httpx","gs-netcat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

    - attack.t1555.003

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'

level: high

Hackers Exploit Gravity SMTP WordPress Plugin Bug to Expose API Keys

The Hacker News
2026-06-20 6 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors are exploiting a recently patched security flaw impacting Gravity SMTP, a WordPress plugin that's installed on about 100,000 sites. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-4020 (CVSS score: 5.3), is a medium-severity information disclosure flaw that can allow unauthenticated attackers to extract sensitive data, such as configuration data, API keys, secrets, and OAuth tokens

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 exploit request to unauthenticated mock-data REST endpoint
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 exploit request to unauthenticated mock-data REST endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP GET requests to the Gravity SMTP plugin REST endpoint /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data, especially carrying the ?page=gravitysmtp-settings parameter that triggers the full System Report disclosure. Article-specific: this exact path+param combination is the documented CVE-2026-4020 weaponization, and Wordfence has blocked 17M+ such requests. Rationale: Keyed on the exact CVE-2026-4020 path /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data and the ?page=gravitysmtp-settings trigger param, both confirmed by BleepingComputer, CrowdSec and SentinelOne as the documented exploit signature; the 10 source IPs are surfaced as enrichment (KnownAttackerIP) since they originate only from the Wordfence advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-info-disclosure-bug-in-gravity-smtp-wordpress-plugin/ • https://www.crowdsec.net/vulntracking-report/cve-2026-4020-gravity-smtp-information-disclosure • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-4020/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-4020
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Wordfence Central, internal pentest tooling) probing the endpoint during scheduled scans
  • Managed-WordPress hosting providers running plugin health/diagnostic checks against wp-json routes
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring tools (UptimeRobot, Pingdom, StatusCake) crawling REST routes
  • Security researchers re-validating the patch after upgrading to 2.1.5
  • Staging/QA traffic from internal CI hitting the same endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not(csUserAgent has_any ("UptimeRobot","Pingdom","StatusCake","WordfenceCentral","WPScan"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all hits for the path, note cIP and whether ?page=gravitysmtp-settings was present and scStatus/scBytes — a 200 with a large body means data was returned; confirm the site's Gravity SMTP version is <2.1.5. 2) Contain: block the offending source IPs at the WAF/edge, update the plugin to 2.1.5+, and immediately rotate ALL configured email-connector credentials (Amazon SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend, Zoho keys/OAuth tokens). 3) Hunt: sweep every web-facing host's logs for the same endpoint, check the 10 known attacker IPs across all sites, and review third-party email-service send logs for unauthorized outbound mail using the exposed keys.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (AttackerIPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.status) as status values(Web.src) as src values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data*" by Web.dest Web.uri_query Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval exploit_param=if(match(uri_query,"(?i)gravitysmtp-settings"),"yes","no") | sort - lastTime
Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 successful System Report disclosure (~365 KB response) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful exploitation of CVE-2026-4020 — an HTTP 200 to /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data returning the ~365 KB JSON System Report that leaks configured email API keys, OAuth tokens and the full software stack. Distinct pivot from the attempt detection: keys on response status + body size to confirm credentials were actually exfiltrated, not just probed. Rationale: Uses the Wordfence-documented ~365 KB response size as the success discriminator (scBytes > 300000 on a 200 to the vulnerable path) — a patched 2.1.5 install or a blocked request will not return the full report, so a large body is a high-fidelity confirmation that API keys were exfiltrated rather than merely probed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-info-disclosure-bug-in-gravity-smtp-wordpress-plugin/ • https://www.crowdsec.net/vulntracking-report/cve-2026-4020-gravity-smtp-information-disclosure • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-4020/
ATT&CKT1552 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest confirming the disclosure with a real 200/large-body response before remediation
  • A legitimately large but benign report body if another route shares the path prefix (mitigated by exact path match)
  • CDN/origin cache revalidation re-serving the full body to a monitoring agent
  • Internal QA explicitly exercising the unpatched endpoint on a staging mirror
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a confirmed disclosure, not an attempt — identify the requesting cIP, the exact timestamp, and which site/host served the 200; treat all email-connector credentials on that site as compromised. 2) Contain: update Gravity SMTP to 2.1.5+, then rotate every Amazon SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend and Zoho key/token configured in the plugin, and revoke any OAuth grants. 3) Hunt: review the third-party email providers' send/auth logs for abuse using the leaked keys, check whether the exposed System Report (plugin versions, paths, DB details) was used to stage follow-on attacks, and confirm no other site in the estate returned a large body from the same endpoint.

| where csUriStem has "/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data"
| where scStatus == 200
| where scBytes > 300000   // ~365 KB full System Report per Wordfence = successful credential disclosure
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, scBytes, csUserAgent
| sort by scBytes desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.src) as src values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent max(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data*" Web.status=200 by Web.dest Web.url _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where bytes_out > 300000 | sort - bytes_out

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/

date: 2026/05/02

        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

level: high

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-4020")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Threat Brief: Mitigating Large-Scale Credential Attacks

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-20 11 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

We provide guidance for preparing for and mitigating large-scale credential attacks, focusing on recent campaigns targeting security vendors' devices. The post Threat Brief: Mitigating Large-Scale Credential Attacks appeared first on Unit 42 .

CVEsCVE-2024-55591 CVE-2025-59718 CVE-2025-59719
ATT&CKT1190 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth · [LLM] FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) · [LLM] FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single source IP producing a high volume of failed authentications against a Fortinet appliance (SSL-VPN / admin login) followed by a successful login in the same window — the exact 'successful logins shortly after large-volume password failure events' pattern Unit 42 flags for the FortiBleed credential-spraying campaign. Rationale: Implements Unit 42's explicit FortiBleed guidance — audit remote-access logs for successful logins shortly after large-volume failure events — scoped to Fortinet auth via the CIM app values / DeviceVendor='Fortinet'. Threshold + same-window success join is what separates spray-then-compromise from routine VPN typos. Cross-checked with SOCRadar/SecurityWeek FortiBleed reporting and Arctic Wolf's CVE-2024-55591 analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote worker repeatedly fat-fingering an SSL-VPN password then succeeding
  • Misconfigured VPN client or saved-credential loop retrying stale creds before a successful re-auth
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Tenable) credential checks against the appliance
  • Shared NAT egress IP where many staff log in (inflated failure+success counts from one SourceIP)
  • Password-rotation day causing widespread first-attempt failures followed by success
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<populate watchlist: known scanner + corp NAT egress IPs via a Sentinel watchlist join, not inline>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CompromisedUser + SourceIP; geolocate SourceIP and check whether the success used MFA and from a known ASN/country. Inspect the failed-user set — many distinct users from one IP = spray, not a typo. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is foreign/unrecognized, force-disable the compromised admin/VPN account, kill active SSL-VPN tunnels, block the SourceIP at the edge, and rotate the credential. 3) Hunt: from that SourceIP/account pivot to post-auth config changes (new admin accounts, sslvpn user groups), jsconsole admin logins, and any config download — feed into the FortiBleed jsconsole and rogue-admin UCs.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 1h;
let Failed = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("failure","failed") or Message has_any ("login failed","Login failed","authentication failed","ssl-login-fail"))
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
let Success = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("success","succeeded") or Message has_any ("login successful","SSL tunnel established"))
| summarize Successes = count(), CompromisedUser = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
Failed
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 = empirical spray burst floor per source per hour
| join kind=inner Success on SourceIP, TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, Failures, TargetUsers, Successes, CompromisedUser
| order by Failures desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate","sslvpn-plain","forticlient_ems") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.action, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1
| sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate","sslvpn-plain","forticlient_ems") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.action, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1
| sort - failures
FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the high-fidelity exploitation signature of CVE-2024-55591: administrative logins attributed to the 'jsconsole' interface and/or successful super-admin logins sourced from the device loopback/local IP — the artifact the Node.js websocket auth-bypass leaves when an unauthenticated attacker forges super_admin access on FortiOS/FortiProxy. Rationale: Uses the two corroborated CVE-2024-55591 exploitation artifacts — `ui=jsconsole` in the admin-login record (matched in CommonSecurityLog Message) and super-admin logins from the device loopback/local IP (CIM Authentication.src=127.0.0.1) — reported by Arctic Wolf, watchTowr ('I Am The Super_Admin Now') and Trustwave. Both are near-zero in benign FortiGate operation. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/get-fortirekt-i-am-the-super_admin-now-fortios-authentication-bypass-cve-2024-55591/ • https://trustwave.com/en-us/resources/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/cve-2024-55591-fortinet-fortios-fortiproxy-zero-day
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately running CLI commands through the FortiGate GUI 'CLI console' widget (also tagged jsconsole) — distinguish by source being a real admin IP, not loopback
  • Automation/orchestration tooling (Ansible/FortiManager) driving CLI via the local console
  • Internal penetration test replicating CVE-2024-55591
  • Health-check scripts hitting the management interface from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the jsconsole/loopback login corresponds to a real admin session — legitimate jsconsole use originates from an authenticated GUI session with a genuine admin SourceIP; exploitation shows loopback/local src and no preceding interactive auth. Check FortiOS version against the CVE-2024-55591 fixed builds. 2) Contain: isolate the device's management interface from the internet, disable/rotate all admin accounts, and capture the running + startup config for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate admin accounts and sslvpn user groups created/modified after the first jsconsole login, look for `--userfrom`-style audit-record tampering, and any config download/exfil to chain with the rogue-admin and FortiBleed config-extraction UCs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has "jsconsole"
| where Message has_any ("login","logged in","logged-in","admin")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, DeviceExternalID, SourceIP, AdminUser = SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, Activity, EventOutcome, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Authentication.dest) as dest from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate") (Authentication.src="127.0.0.1" OR Authentication.src="0.0.0.0" OR Authentication.src="::1") by Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Authentication.dest) as dest from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate") (Authentication.src="127.0.0.1" OR Authentication.src="0.0.0.0" OR Authentication.src="::1") by Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - firstTime
FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts post-exploitation persistence for the FortiBleed/CVE-2024-55591 chain: creation of new FortiGate administrator accounts (often random usernames) or new SSL-VPN local users / user groups via config changes. This is how attackers convert a one-shot auth bypass into durable, high-privilege access for offline-cracked credential re-use. Rationale: Targets the documented CVE-2024-55591 post-exploit actions — new admin accounts with random names, new SSL-VPN local users and groups — via Fortinet config-change logs (cfgpath system.admin / user.group) and the CIM Change datamodel (action=created, object_category=user). Account creation on an edge appliance is rare and tightly change-controlled, so FP is low. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf and Cyble. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://cyble.com/blog/cve-2024-55591-the-fortinet-flaw-putting-critical-systems-at-risk/
ATT&CKT1136 T1098 T1133
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned admin onboarding by the network team during a change window
  • FortiManager/automation pushing a config template that provisions admin or VPN users
  • Legitimate SSL-VPN user-group expansion during an access-request rollout
  • MSP/managed-SOC provisioning a monitoring admin account
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ActorAdmin and SourceIP that created the new object; correlate against an authorized change ticket and verify the actor session was not a jsconsole/loopback exploit login. Flag random-looking usernames. 2) Contain: delete or disable the unauthorized admin/VPN account and group, terminate its sessions, and rotate credentials for every legitimate admin on the device. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account granted VPN access, established tunnels into internal networks, or downloaded the device config; pivot on its SourceIP across other edge devices to scope the FortiBleed campaign footprint.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has_any ("system.admin","user.local","user.group")
| where Message has_any ("super_admin","prof_admin","accprofile","sslvpn")
| where Message has_any ("Object attribute configured","Added","cfgattr","New","create")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, ActorAdmin = SourceUserName, NewObject = DestinationHostName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, values(All_Changes.user) as actor, values(All_Changes.command) as command from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action=created All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.vendor_product IN ("Fortinet FortiGate","FortiGate","FortiOS","Fortinet FortiProxy") by All_Changes.dest, All_Changes.object
| `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
| `ctime(firstTime)`
| sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, values(All_Changes.user) as actor, values(All_Changes.command) as command from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action=created All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.vendor_product IN ("Fortinet FortiGate","FortiGate","FortiOS","Fortinet FortiProxy") by All_Changes.dest, All_Changes.object
| `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
| `ctime(firstTime)`
| sort - firstTime
FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed campaign's parallel targeting of internet-exposed MSSQL: a single client IP generating a burst of SQL Server login failures (error 18456) across one or many logins within a short window — the spray signature Unit 42 observed against MSSQL devices alongside Fortinet and Sophos. Rationale: Covers the article's explicit observation that the FortiBleed actors also targeted MSSQL devices. Pivots on SQL Server error 18456 (login failed) parsed for CLIENT IP and login name in Sentinel's Event table, with a Defender DeviceLogonEvents fallback for Windows-auth brute force against the SQL host and a CIM Authentication path for Splunk. Threshold-based, so framed as a burst detector. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application/service account with a stale connection string hammering the DB after a password change
  • Linked-server or ETL job misconfigured with wrong credentials retrying in a tight loop
  • Monitoring agent (SCOM/SolarWinds) probing SQL with expired creds
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner credential audit against the SQL instance
  • Developer load-test pointing at the wrong SQL host
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("sqlmonitor","svc-etl","svc-backup")   // tune to your known SQL service accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve ClientIP — internal app server vs external/unknown. Inspect the targeted login set: many distinct logins from one IP = spray; a single service account = likely stale credential. Check for any 18454/successful login from the same ClientIP right after the burst. 2) Contain: if external, block the ClientIP at the firewall, confirm the SQL instance is not directly internet-exposed, and disable SQL-auth logins that were sprayed; enforce that MSSQL sits behind the VPN/jump box. 3) Hunt: if a success followed, review that login's subsequent activity (xp_cmdshell, new SQL logins, linked-server abuse) and pivot the ClientIP across Fortinet edge logs to tie it to the broader FortiBleed spraying infrastructure.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| where LogonType in ("Network","Batch")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedAccounts = dcount(AccountName), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 30), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 failed network logons / 30 min from one source = spray
| order by Failures desc
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 30m;
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Source == "MSSQLSERVER"
| where EventID == 18456   // SQL Server: Login failed
| extend LoginUser = extract(@"Login failed for user '([^']+)'", 1, RenderedDescription)
| extend ClientIP = extract(@"\[CLIENT: ([0-9A-Fa-f\.:]+)\]", 1, RenderedDescription)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP)
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedLogins = dcount(LoginUser), Logins = make_set(LoginUser, 30) by ClientIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where Failures >= 30
| order by Failures desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("mssqlserver","mssql","sqlserver","microsoft sql server") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(count) as failures, dc(user) as targeted_logins, values(user) as logins by src, _time
| where failures >= 30
| sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("mssqlserver","mssql","sqlserver","microsoft sql server") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(count) as failures, dc(user) as targeted_logins, values(user) as logins by src, _time
| where failures >= 30
| sort - failures
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-59718", "CVE-2025-59719")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-59718", "CVE-2025-59719")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] OpenRemote alarm-endpoint authorization-failure cascade then success (IDOR boundary probing) · [LLM] OpenRemote alarm-ID enumeration via 404-response probing across realms
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] OpenRemote cross-realm alarm DELETE: single client deleting alarms in >1 realm (IDOR)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OpenRemote high-volume alarm DELETE to /api/*/alarm (mass destruction / scripted abuse)
OpenRemote cross-realm alarm DELETE: single client deleting alarms in >1 realm (IDOR) AIExploitation High
Hunts the core removeAlarms IDOR (GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf): a single authenticated client issuing DELETE requests to /api/{realm}/alarm for more than one distinct realm. In OpenRemote a normal tenant user operates within exactly one realm, so any source touching alarm deletions across multiple realm paths is the defining cross-tenant exploitation signal. Rationale: Pivots on the exact vulnerable shape — DELETE to /api/{realm}/alarm (PoC: DELETE /api/smartcity/alarm) — and on the realm path segment that OpenRemote routing confirms is the first /api/ token. dcount(realm)>1 per client is the cleanest expression of cross-tenant IDOR with no need for an external realm-to-user ACL mapping. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf • https://docs.openremote.io/docs/architecture/manager-endpoints-and-file-paths/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/io.openremote/openremote-manager/CVE-2026-41166/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Master-realm superadmin legitimately managing alarms across all tenants (OpenRemote's superuser operates cross-realm by design)
  • MSP / managed-service operator account provisioned with multi-realm scope
  • Automated alarm-retention/housekeeping service account with cross-realm permissions
  • Multiple tenants' admins egressing through a shared corporate NAT IP so distinct legit users collapse to one SourceIP when SourceUserName is not forwarded by the proxy
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the client (SourceUserName if forwarded, else SourceIP) and list the realms hit and how many DELETEs returned 2xx. Pull the caller's actual home realm/role from OpenRemote Keycloak; a tenant user with WRITE_ALARMS_ROLE hitting other realms is exploitation, not admin work. 2) Contain: revoke/disable the offending Keycloak account and its sessions, block the SourceIP at the proxy/WAF, and confirm OpenRemote Manager is upgraded to >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: enumerate which victim realms lost alarms, restore from DB backup, and review the same client for prior 404-probing (enumeration) and 401/403 boundary-testing in the preceding hour.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "DELETE"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"/api/[^/?]+/alarm"
| extend Realm = extract(@"/api/([^/?]+)/alarm", 1, RequestURL)
| where isnotempty(Realm)
| summarize Requests=count(), Realms=make_set(Realm), RealmCount=dcount(Realm), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, SourceUserName
| where RealmCount > 1
| sort by RealmCount desc, Requests desc
source:nginx @http.method:DELETE @http.url_details.path:/api/*/alarm

OpenRemote high-volume alarm DELETE to /api/*/alarm (mass destruction / scripted abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single client issuing a high volume of successful DELETE requests to the OpenRemote alarm endpoint in a short window — the impact phase of the removeAlarms IDOR where an attacker scripts repeated bulk deletes to permanently destroy safety-critical and security alarms. Note a single request can carry many IDs in its body, so request-rate is a conservative lower bound on damage. Rationale: Targets the article's bulk-delete impact using the concrete endpoint (/api/{realm}/alarm) and successful (2xx) responses. Threshold of 20 successful DELETEs per 10 min flags scripted/automated destruction; because the IDs live in the request body (not logged), request count is a deliberate proxy and pairs with the cross-realm UC for confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf • https://docs.openremote.io/docs/architecture/manager-endpoints-and-file-paths/
ATT&CKT1485 T1190

  • Operator clearing an alarm storm after a faulty sensor or integration flooded the realm
  • Admin removing test/staging alarms during a deployment or onboarding
  • Realm decommission / data migration that legitimately purges alarms
  • A UI 'clear all' action that fans out into many sequential DELETE calls
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the client's role/realm in Keycloak and whether the destroyed alarms belong to the caller's own realm; cross-check the same window for realm_count>1 (cross-realm UC). 2) Contain: if the account is a tenant user deleting outside scope or unrecognized automation, disable the account/sessions, block the SourceIP, and verify the build is >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: quantify deleted alarms per realm from the DB audit/backup, restore safety-critical alarms, and look back for the enumeration (404 probing) and authorization-failure cascade that typically precede the destructive burst.

OpenRemote alarm-endpoint authorization-failure cascade then success (IDOR boundary probing) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects the probe-and-exploit pattern characteristic of IDOR discovery: a single client receiving multiple 401/403 responses on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm and then succeeding (2xx) within the same short window. This surfaces an attacker systematically testing which realms/IDs they can reach before landing a working cross-tenant delete. Rationale: Uses the article's stated probe semantics (authorization errors on restricted realms followed by successes on exploitable ones) against the specific DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm endpoint. Same-bucket failure+success per client is a high-signal boundary-testing shape that generic alarm activity does not produce. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A partially-privileged user who legitimately hits some forbidden alarms (403) then deletes ones they own (2xx)
  • A buggy/retrying API client that re-sends after token refresh produces 401 then 200
  • A Keycloak role/permission change mid-session flipping 403 to 200
  • Pen-test / authorized vulnerability scan against the OpenRemote instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: order the client's requests by time and confirm the 401/403 -> 2xx transition is against different realm IDs (probing) rather than one resource retried after auth refresh. 2) Contain: disable the account/sessions and block the SourceIP if probing across realms is confirmed; verify the instance is patched to >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: pull the full request sequence for this client to map which realms were probed vs. successfully deleted, then check for 404-based ID enumeration and high-volume deletes from the same source.

| sort by AuthFailures desc

OpenRemote alarm-ID enumeration via 404-response probing across realms AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects cross-tenant alarm enumeration: a single client generating many 404 responses on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm, optionally while rotating realm paths. The advisory states presence of sequential auto-increment alarm IDs is confirmed by 404-vs-200 responses, so a burst of 404s on this endpoint is the discovery footprint that precedes targeted destruction. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's enumeration mechanism (sequential @GeneratedValue IDs confirmed by 404 vs 200). A high 404 count on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm from one client (amplified when realm_count>1) is a distinct discovery pivot separate from the impact/volume detections. Langflow file-ingestion endpoint receives archive/bundle upload (CVE-2026-55447 delivery) AIDelivery Low
Hunts POST uploads to Langflow's file-ingestion API (/api/v1/files/upload, /api/v2/files) that feed BaseFileComponent nodes (Read File, Docling, Unstructured, etc.). CVE-2026-55447 is delivered by uploading a TAR bundle whose symlink members point at arbitrary absolute paths, so the upload itself is the first observable step. Reverse-proxy/WAF logs are the only place this inbound request is visible. Rationale: Uses the concrete Langflow upload endpoints (/api/v1/files/upload, /api/v2/files) from the docs the advisory references; these feed the BaseFileComponent nodes the article lists. Low fidelity alone (legit RAG document uploads look identical at the proxy layer with no body inspection), so it is a delivery-phase pivot to correlate with the host-side UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7273426 • https://docs.langflow.org/api-files
ATT&CKT1190 T1659
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading documents/datasets into RAG ingestion flows
  • Automated/scheduled ingestion pipelines or ETL jobs seeding vector stores
  • CI/CD or demo seeding of flows via the files API
  • Bulk dataset migration uploads by data engineers
  • Synthetic monitoring / health-check probes hitting the files endpoint
Suppression filter
| where DestinationServiceName !has "healthcheck" and SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP, user-agent and authenticated principal for the upload; confirm whether the source is an expected internal ingestion service or an unknown/external client. 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, block it at the WAF/reverse proxy and pivot to the Langflow host to check whether the host-side symlink/sensitive-file-read UC fired in the same window; if confirmed, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: on the Langflow host, look for the worker reading secret_key/etc/shadow/.ssh/.aws (UC2) and the Python worker spawning shells (UC3) within minutes of this upload; rotate LANGFLOW_SECRET_KEY and any exposed credentials and confirm the instance is >= 1.9.2.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/v1/files/upload", "/api/v2/files", "/api/v1/files")
| summarize Uploads = count(), Paths = make_set(RequestURL, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 10) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationServiceName
| order by Uploads desc
